doc.title: Dorothy Donegan — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Pianists rated: Monk, Phineas Newborn, Bud Powell, Ahmad Jamal, Cecil Taylor
summary: Monk the innovator, Newborn challenging her with fast light playing, Powell great before his decline, Jamal loved, and Cecil Taylor a technician she would outshine.

story.theme_name: Pianists: who played, who influenced whom
story.community_name: Who played piano: the pianists musicians remembered

blocks.x: Thelonious Monk.
He was an innovator.
How so?
He played different from everybody else. He was a creator.
Phineas Newborn.
He was a genius. He could play light and fast. He’d come over and challenge me all the time.
And how would those competitions go, those challenges?
I would hang in there with him. I put one of those concertos on him.
And? Did he make it, did he live up to your high standards?
Well, I liked him anyway. ‘Cause he could play in the bass with two hands, that running bass (sings). I liked him.
How about Bud Powell?
He was great, too.
In what way? How did his greatness differ from some of these other players?
I don’t know. But me and Erroll Garner heard him during his last days and he wasn’t doing too well, but I admired him when he was right. When he and Buttercup were together, you know.
How about Ahmad Jamal?
Oh, I love him.
What do you love about him?
I like the way he plays. I like Fritz. That’s his real name, you know.
How about Cecil Taylor?

He’s a screwball but he got a lot of technique. They wanted to put me and him together you know, they had done it with Mary Lou. So I told ‘em, I said, “I’ll steal that show if I have to pull up my dress.”
